quote: Propranolol 20–40 mg BID — a non-selective beta-blocker with the strongest evidence base for akathisia from multiple small RCTs and Cochrane review.
problem: The keyed option says propranolol has the 'strongest evidence base' and cites the Cochrane review in support. The item's own rationale says the Cochrane review found the data insufficient to recommend beta-blockers. Two recent network meta-analyses find larger effects for low-dose mirtazapine and other 5-HT2A antagonists. The prior finding A1C1-F002 was fixed in the rationale only; the option still makes the same claim.
whyItMatters: The item contradicts itself. A learner reading the keyed option will believe the Cochrane review supports propranolol and that nothing has better evidence, and will not think of mirtazapine as an evidence-based alternative.
evidence: Lima AR et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2004 (CD001946): 3 small RCTs, n=51, no firm conclusions, data insufficient to recommend beta-blockers. Gerolymos C et al., JAMA Netw Open 2024;7(3):e241527 (doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.1527), NMA of 15 RCTs: mirtazapine 15 mg (SMD -1.20), biperiden, vitamin B6 largest effects; propranolol SMD -0.78, not robust in sensitivity analyses. Furukawa Y et al., Schizophr Bull 2026 (doi:10.1093/schbul/sbae098), NMA of 19 RCTs: 5-HT2A antagonists SMD -1.07 vs beta-blockers SMD -0.46, both low-certainty evidence.
correction: Propranolol 20–40 mg BID — a lipophilic non-selective beta-blocker and the conventional first-line add-on for akathisia, although its trial evidence is small and low-certainty.
verified: PubMed: retrieved metadata/abstracts for PMIDs 38451521 and 38869177; Cochrane result recalled and also stated in this item's own rationale.

quote: Which pharmacological intervention has the strongest evidence as first-line treatment for akathisia in this setting?
problem: The stem asks which agent has the 'strongest evidence'. The keyed agent, propranolol, does not have the strongest evidence: 5-HT2A antagonists such as mirtazapine show larger effects in both 2024–2026 network meta-analyses. Propranolol is the right key among the options offered, but not for the reason the stem asks about.
whyItMatters: The stem teaches that propranolol is supported by the best evidence, which the current literature does not show.
evidence: Lima AR et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2004 (CD001946): 3 small RCTs, n=51, no firm conclusions, data insufficient to recommend beta-blockers. Gerolymos C et al., JAMA Netw Open 2024;7(3):e241527 (doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.1527), NMA of 15 RCTs: mirtazapine 15 mg (SMD -1.20), biperiden, vitamin B6 largest effects; propranolol SMD -0.78, not robust in sensitivity analyses. Furukawa Y et al., Schizophr Bull 2026 (doi:10.1093/schbul/sbae098), NMA of 19 RCTs: 5-HT2A antagonists SMD -1.07 vs beta-blockers SMD -0.46, both low-certainty evidence.
correction: Which pharmacological intervention is the most appropriate first-line add-on treatment for akathisia in this setting?
verified: PubMed: retrieved metadata/abstracts for PMIDs 38451521 and 38869177; Cochrane result recalled and also stated in this item's own rationale.

quote: Akathisia pharmacotherapy: propranolol 20–40 mg BID is first-line (strongest evidence)
problem: The pearl repeats 'strongest evidence' for propranolol. The item's rationale and current network meta-analyses contradict this.
whyItMatters: The pearl is shown as a standalone takeaway, so it will be remembered without the rationale's caveat.
evidence: Lima AR et al., Cochrane Database Syst Rev 2004 (CD001946): 3 small RCTs, n=51, no firm conclusions, data insufficient to recommend beta-blockers. Gerolymos C et al., JAMA Netw Open 2024;7(3):e241527 (doi:10.1001/jamanetworkopen.2024.1527), NMA of 15 RCTs: mirtazapine 15 mg (SMD -1.20), biperiden, vitamin B6 largest effects; propranolol SMD -0.78, not robust in sensitivity analyses. Furukawa Y et al., Schizophr Bull 2026 (doi:10.1093/schbul/sbae098), NMA of 19 RCTs: 5-HT2A antagonists SMD -1.07 vs beta-blockers SMD -0.46, both low-certainty evidence.
correction: Akathisia pharmacotherapy: after dose reduction or switch, propranolol 20–40 mg BID is the conventional first-line add-on (low-certainty evidence; low-dose mirtazapine is an evidence-based alternative)
verified: PubMed: retrieved metadata/abstracts for PMIDs 38451521 and 38869177; Cochrane result recalled and also stated in this item's own rationale.

quote: Social anxiety disorder, Performance type requiring PRN medication
problem: DSM-5-TR calls this specifier 'performance only', not 'Performance type'. 'Requiring PRN medication' also overstates the case: a PRN beta-blocker is an option, and CBT/exposure is effective too.
whyItMatters: Learners may write a specifier that does not exist, and may believe medication is mandatory for performance-only social anxiety.
evidence: DSM-5-TR, social anxiety disorder (300.23/F40.10), specifier 'Specify if: Performance only: if the fear is restricted to speaking or performing in public.'
correction: Social anxiety disorder, performance only — a PRN beta-blocker is a reasonable option

quote: Risperidone and aripiprazole are FDA-approved for irritability and aggression associated with autism — they do not treat
problem: The FDA approvals for irritability associated with autistic disorder are pediatric only: risperidone for ages 5–16 and aripiprazole for ages 6–17. The patient in the stem is 18, so for him either drug is off-label. The keyed answer implies an approval that does not cover his age.
whyItMatters: Learners will think these drugs are on-label for autistic adults. They may tell families so and document an FDA indication that does not exist.
evidence: Risperdal (risperidone) USPI: irritability associated with autistic disorder in pediatric patients 5–16 years (approved 2006). Abilify (aripiprazole) USPI: irritability associated with autistic disorder in pediatric patients 6–17 years (approved 2009).
correction: Risperidone and aripiprazole are FDA-approved for irritability (including aggression and self-injury) associated with autism in children and adolescents (risperidone 5–16 years, aripiprazole 6–17 years; use at 18 is off-label) — they do not treat

quote: Symptoms before age 12 with impairment in at least two settings
problem: 'Impairment in at least two settings' is the DSM-IV wording (criterion C). DSM-5 and DSM-5-TR require several symptoms to be present in two or more settings (C), plus clear evidence of functional interference (D). Impairment does not have to occur in two settings.
whyItMatters: This is a shelf-tested criterion. Learners will memorize the superseded DSM-IV rule and may wrongly exclude ADHD when impairment is concentrated in one setting.
evidence: DSM-5-TR ADHD Criterion C: 'Several inattentive or hyperactive-impulsive symptoms are present in two or more settings'; Criterion D: 'clear evidence that the symptoms interfere with, or reduce the quality of, social, academic, or occupational functioning.' DSM-IV-TR Criterion C read 'Some impairment from the symptoms is present in two or more settings.'
correction: Several symptoms before age 12, present in at least two settings, with evidence of functional impairment

quote: ADHD requires several symptoms before age 12, ≥6 months, with impairment in ≥2 settings
problem: The rationale repeats the DSM-IV 'impairment in two settings' wording. It also omits the symptom-count threshold.
evidence: DSM-5-TR ADHD Criteria A–D (≥6 symptoms, ≥5 for age 17+; several before age 12; several present in ≥2 settings; clear functional interference).
correction: ADHD requires ≥6 symptoms (≥5 at age 17+) for ≥6 months, several present before age 12 and several present in ≥2 settings, with clear functional impairment

quote: A child is evaluated for intellectual disability.
problem: DSM-5-TR renamed the disorder 'intellectual developmental disorder (intellectual disability)', aligning with ICD-11.
whyItMatters: A minor currency gap. The keyed content (severity graded by adaptive functioning) is correct.
evidence: DSM-5-TR (2022), Neurodevelopmental Disorders: 'Intellectual Developmental Disorder (Intellectual Disability)'.
correction: A child is evaluated for intellectual developmental disorder (intellectual disability).

quote: A specific, credible threat to a named, identifiable person — with described means and timeline — triggers a duty to take reasonable protective steps.
problem: The item teaches a duty to protect as a universal obligation. It never says that duty-to-warn/protect law varies by state: mandatory in some states, permissive in others (disclosure allowed but not required), and not recognized in a few (e.g., Texas, Thapar v. Zezulka 1999). The stem asks for 'the therapist's obligation', and neither the rationale nor the pearl mentions state variation. qb_eth_007 does hedge.
whyItMatters: The curriculum is meant for national use. A learner will assume one rule applies everywhere and may misstate the legal basis for a disclosure. The clinical action (protective steps for a credible, specific threat) is still sound everywhere.
evidence: Tarasoff v. Regents (Cal. 1976); state duty-to-protect statutes vary (e.g., NCSL/APA state surveys: mandatory vs permissive vs no duty); Thapar v. Zezulka, 997 S.W.2d 635 (Tex. 1999).
correction: A specific, credible threat to a named, identifiable person — with described means and timeline — triggers a duty to take reasonable protective steps in most states (mandatory in some, permissive in others; know your state's statute).

quote: Commitment status and medication consent are independent legal states.
problem: This is presented as universal. Most states separate commitment from the authority to medicate over objection. A minority, however, build an incapacity-to-consent-to-treatment finding into the commitment criteria, so commitment itself carries treatment authority (Utah's commitment standard is one example).
whyItMatters: A learner in a state with a treatment-inclusive commitment standard would misunderstand what their commitment order authorizes. The keyed answer is still correct for most US jurisdictions.
evidence: State civil-commitment statutes vary; e.g., Utah Code §26B-5-332 commitment criteria include that the person lacks the ability to engage in a rational decision-making process regarding treatment. Rennie v. Klein and Rogers v. Okin established the separate-process model in other jurisdictions.
correction: In most states, commitment status and medication consent are independent legal states (a few states build an incapacity finding into the commitment criteria — know your state's rule).
verified: recall — the specific Utah statute section should be confirmed

quote: Informed consent = capacity + disclosure + voluntariness — all three must be documented; 'intact cognition' is not the same as a documented capacity assessment.
problem: The pearl implies every informed consent needs a formally documented four-ability capacity assessment. Adults are presumed to have capacity, and a formal assessment is triggered by clinical concern. The real gap in the stem is that 'I understand' is self-report and does not show understanding or appreciation, which matters for ECT in a severely depressed patient.
whyItMatters: Learners may either treat formal capacity documentation as a routine requirement of every consent, or miss the actual lesson: check understanding and appreciation (e.g., teach-back) when illness may impair them.
evidence: Appelbaum PS, NEJM 2007 'Assessment of patients' competence to consent to treatment' (presumption of capacity; assessment triggered by clinical indicators); APA Task Force on ECT (2001), consent section.
correction: Informed consent = capacity + disclosure + voluntariness; adults are presumed capable, but 'intact cognition' and 'I understand' do not show understanding and appreciation — for a high-stakes consent such as ECT, check them (e.g., teach-back) and document it.

problem: Child-abuse reporting duties are close to uniform across states, but elder and dependent-adult reporting duties are not. Who must report, and in which settings, varies. New York, for example, has no general mandatory elder-abuse reporting for physicians outside residential care facilities.
whyItMatters: A learner may believe a mandated duty (and the protection that comes with it) exists wherever they practise, and may disclose without checking the local legal basis.
evidence: State adult protective services statutes vary (e.g., NCEA state law summaries; New York has no universal mandated reporting of elder abuse in community settings).
correction: Elder/dependent-adult abuse carries similar duties in most states, though who must report and in which settings varies by state.

quote: he also has racing thoughts, psychomotor agitation, and is sleeping only 3 hours per night despite feeling exhausted
problem: The stem's 'mixed features' rests on racing thoughts, psychomotor agitation, and insomnia with exhaustion. DSM-5-TR's 'with mixed features' specifier requires ≥3 non-overlapping manic/hypomanic symptoms. It explicitly excludes psychomotor agitation, and it counts only decreased need for sleep (feeling rested), not insomnia. The patient therefore has one qualifying symptom and does not meet the specifier the keyed answer names.
whyItMatters: Learners will label agitated depression with insomnia as 'mixed features'. That is a misapplied DSM-5-TR specifier, and it can push toward a bipolar-spectrum formulation. The item's safety message about agitation and suicide risk is sound; the criteria are not.
evidence: DSM-5-TR, depressive disorders, 'With mixed features' specifier: at least three of seven manic/hypomanic symptoms, including 'decreased need for sleep (feeling rested despite sleeping less than usual; to be contrasted with insomnia)'. Note: overlapping symptoms (psychomotor agitation, irritability, distractibility, insomnia) are excluded.
correction: he also has racing thoughts, pressured speech, and increased goal-directed activity, and is sleeping only 3 hours per night yet feels rested

quote: Mixed features (depression + racing thoughts/agitation/decreased sleep) carry elevated suicide risk
problem: The pearl lists agitation as a mixed-features symptom, but DSM-5-TR excludes it as an overlapping symptom. It also needs ≥3 manic symptoms. (The linked page's evidence line, 'depressed mood with concurrent activation/agitation', has the same framing.)
whyItMatters: It teaches the wrong specifier criteria as a standalone takeaway.
correction: Mixed features (depression + ≥3 non-overlapping manic symptoms such as racing thoughts, pressured speech, or decreased need for sleep — not agitation or insomnia, which DSM-5-TR excludes) carry elevated suicide risk

quote: the alert, attentive patient without fluctuating consciousness rules out delirium.
problem: A single exam showing intact attention cannot rule out delirium, which by definition fluctuates and is often hypoactive in older adults. For a 70-year-old with new-onset psychosis, the standard is serial assessment plus a medical and neurocognitive workup.
whyItMatters: A learner may stop delirium screening and the medical workup in an elderly patient after one normal exam, which is a can't-miss diagnosis on the geriatric unit.
evidence: DSM-5-TR delirium Criterion B ('tends to fluctuate in severity during the course of a day'); APA Practice Guideline on delirium / NICE CG103.
correction: the alert, attentive patient makes delirium less likely — though one exam cannot exclude a fluctuating course, so reassess and complete the medical workup.

quote: None of these criteria are met.
problem: The item says 'continued inpatient care is indicated' and marks 'the right to leave AMA' as the 'Autonomy over safety' error. It never says that a voluntary patient's discharge request is governed by state law. A missing safety plan and an unscheduled appointment are tasks for the team to finish, not grounds to hold someone. Mood has also partly improved, so 'none' is inaccurate.
whyItMatters: Learners may believe a voluntary patient can be kept because paperwork is incomplete, which is unlawful detention unless involuntary criteria are met and the state's process is followed.
evidence: State voluntary-admission statutes (e.g., written release request → discharge within a statutory window unless involuntary proceedings are initiated); APA Position Statement on involuntary hospitalization.
correction: None of these criteria are fully met, so the team should recommend he stay — but if a voluntary patient still requests discharge, state law decides: without grounds for an involuntary hold, he is discharged, with the safety plan and follow-up completed before he leaves rather than used as a reason to hold him.

quote: ECT with appropriate obstetric monitoring avoids this entirely.
problem: ECT does not avoid fetal drug exposure 'entirely'. Every session involves an induction anesthetic (e.g., methohexital/propofol), a depolarizing muscle relaxant, and often an anticholinergic, all of which cross the placenta. The advantage is brief, intermittent exposure instead of continuous psychotropic exposure.
whyItMatters: Learners may tell a pregnant patient that ECT involves no drug exposure, which is inaccurate informed-consent information.
evidence: APA Task Force on ECT (2001), pregnancy section; ACOG/APA perinatal guidance; standard ECT anesthesia practice.
correction: ECT limits fetal drug exposure to brief anesthetic and muscle-relaxant doses at each session rather than continuous psychotropic exposure.

quote: pregnancy is an explicit ECT indication when medications are undesirable
problem: The keyed option calls pregnancy (when medications are undesirable) an explicit ECT indication. The item's own rationale and the linked page say the opposite: 'Pregnancy alone is not the indication; the severity is.' The option therefore contradicts the rationale.
whyItMatters: Learners may believe that a preference to avoid medication in pregnancy is enough to justify ECT for depression of any severity.
evidence: t_mood.md as quoted in this item's evidence line; this item's rationale ('it is not an indication on its own').
correction: ECT is preferred once illness in pregnancy is this severe

quote: explicitly indicated when medications are undesirable — especially when there is active suicidality, refusal to eat, or prior ECT response.
problem: The pearl repeats the 'indicated when medications are undesirable' framing that the rationale rejects.
whyItMatters: The standalone pearl carries the same contradiction.
correction: preferred when the illness is severe (active suicidality, refusal to eat, psychosis) or there is a prior ECT response — pregnancy alone is not the indication.
